Vocabulary · Flyblown and distorted

Select six synonyms of flyblown.

Check the six words

wormy, unhealthy, worm-eaten, contaminated, maggoty, infested.

These suggest something spoiled, unhealthy or affected by pests.

Is distorted used correctly? Choose True or False.

Check True or False

True, True, False.

A view can be inaccurate and a reflection can change shape. An accurate record is not distorted.

Which word does not belong?

distorted, unrecognisable, precise, grotesque

Check the answer

Precise. It means exact or accurate.

Complete the sentences with flyblown or distorted.

Check the answers

Flyblown food; distorted image.

The food is spoiled. The ripples change the shape of the reflection.

1. A neglected garden

Setting · mood · atmosphere

the fence around the court had holes in it and the net had mostly rotted away

Which details make the garden feel neglected rather than carefully looked after?

Check the answer

The damaged fence and rotting net show neglect: they have been left in poor condition.

How could this setting make an ordinary home feel strange?

Think about: Name the detail that seems uncared for. Explain what it suggests about the garden. Say how this could make the place feel strange.

Reveal model answer

The words “holes in it” and “mostly rotted away” suggest that the garden has not been cared for. A tennis court is usually a place for people to play, but this one seems abandoned. This makes the home feel strange because a familiar place for fun now feels empty and forgotten.

2. At home, but busy

Character analysis · relationships

“Read a book,” said her mother. “Watch a video. Play with your toys.”
“And leave me alone to work.”

What best describes Coraline’s parents during the rainy-day conversations?

Check the answer

They want to work while Coraline occupies herself. Her father directly asks to be left alone to work.

How might their responses help explain Coraline’s wish to explore?

Think about: Explain what her mother suggests and what her father asks. Think about what Coraline wants instead. Link their responses to her decision to explore.

Reveal model answer

Her mother suggests books, videos and toys, while her father asks her to “leave me alone to work”. These responses leave Coraline to find something to do by herself. She is bored with her usual activities and wants to explore, so investigating the flat gives her the interest and excitement she is looking for.

3. Who lives where?

Character analysis · contrast

“It’s Coraline. Not Caroline. Coraline,” said Coraline.

Sort the neighbours’ traits.

Upstairs, downstairs or both?

Check the answer

Upstairs: man; Coraline thinks he is making things up; claims to keep trained mice. Both: old; call her Caroline. Downstairs: Highland terriers; round; former actresses.

What do the neighbours’ mistakes with her name suggest about how Coraline is treated?

Think about: Notice the name the neighbours use. Explain why Coraline repeats her correct name. What does this suggest about whether they listen carefully?

Reveal model answer

The neighbours call her Caroline instead of Coraline. She repeats “Coraline” to make her correct name clear. This suggests that they have not listened carefully enough to get her name right and that she wants them to pay attention to her.

4. Through Coraline’s eyes

Narrative viewpoint · character

Coraline didn’t think there really was a mouse circus. She thought the old man was probably making it up.

Which narrative viewpoint does Chapter 1 use?

Check the answer

Third-person limited. The narrator uses Coraline’s name and tells us her thoughts, without revealing everyone else’s thoughts.

How does following Coraline’s thoughts affect what we know about the house?

Think about: Name one thought we know Coraline has. Explain what we still do not know about the man’s story. How does that leave a mystery for the reader?

Reveal model answer

We know that Coraline thinks the man is “probably making it up”. However, we do not know whether there really is a mouse circus, because we only know her view of it. Following her thoughts leaves us with the same uncertainty as Coraline and makes the house seem mysterious.

5. A door to nowhere?

Door motif · suspense

She was sure that her mother had shut the door,but now it was ever so slightly open.Just a crack.

At the end of Chapter 1, what has changed?

Check the answer

The door is slightly open, although the brick wall remains. Coraline does not know what opened it.

Why does the door become more mysterious each time Coraline notices it?

Think about: Think about the locked door, the brick wall and the door being open at night. What question does each discovery make Coraline or the reader ask?

Reveal model answer

At first the locked door makes Coraline wonder where it leads. Then the brick wall makes her wonder why there is a door to nowhere. Later it is “ever so slightly open”, which makes us ask who or what opened it. Each discovery creates another question, so the door becomes harder to explain.

6. A rock, or a toad?

Stone imagery · appearances

a rock that looked just like a frog, and a toad that looked just like a rock.

Which observation shows that appearances can be misleading?

Check the answer

A rock looks like an animal, and an animal looks like a rock. Their appearance could make someone mistake one thing for another.

How does the rock and toad description show that you cannot always trust what you see?

Think about: Explain what the rock looks like and what the toad looks like. Name the mistake someone could make. What does this show about first impressions?

Reveal model answer

The rock looks like a frog, but it is not alive. The toad looks like a rock, but it is an animal. Someone looking quickly could mistake the rock for an animal and the toad for a stone. This shows that first impressions can be wrong: looking like something does not make it that thing.

7. The rat song

Rat motif · sound · threatening atmosphere

We are small but we are many
We are many we are small
We were here before you rose
We will be here when you fall.

What is the song’s rhyme scheme?

Check the answer

ABCB. “Many” is A, “small” is B, “rose” is C and “fall” is B because it rhymes with “small”.

Why do the words “many” and “we” make the creatures sound powerful? What makes the last line threatening?

Think about: Explain “many”, then “we”. Finally, explain what “when you fall” seems to promise. Connect each part to power or threat.

Reveal model answer

“Many” suggests that there are lots of creatures, so their numbers make them powerful even though they are small. “We” suggests that they are united and speaking as one group. “When you fall” sounds threatening because they speak as if Coraline’s defeat is certain. Saying they will still be there suggests that they expect to outlast her.

8. How unease builds

Sequence · changing atmosphere

It was little more than a shadow,and it scuttled down the darkened hall fast, like a little patch of night.

Put the events in order.

Check the answer

First she explores the grounds. Then her father suggests counting things indoors. She finds the locked door, and her mother reveals the wall. After the microwave pizza, she follows the shadow at night.

When does the chapter begin to feel tense or frightening? Use words from the text to explain your answer.

Think about: Choose a moment when you feel tense. Quote a word or phrase from that moment. Explain what it makes you imagine and what you want to find out.

Reveal model answer

The chapter feels tense when Coraline follows the dark shape at night. “Scuttled” makes me imagine something moving quickly, and “a little patch of night” makes it seem like a piece of darkness is moving along the hall. I want to know what the shape is and where it is going. These unanswered questions create suspense.

Title, main idea and figurative phrases

What would be a good title for Chapter 1?

This Dinner Again · An Unfriendly Black Cat · The Fairy Garden · A Strange New Home

Check the title

A Strange New Home. It covers the setting and Coraline’s unusual discoveries.

What is the main idea of Chapter 1?

Check the main idea

Coraline discovers a strange locked door as she entertains herself exploring her new home.

Write another figurative phrase with a similar meaning.

Reveal examples

“We trod the boards.” → “Strut one’s stuff.”

“Trod the boards” means acted on stage. “Strut one’s stuff” means show off your skill or perform confidently.

“It’s bucketing down.” → “It’s raining cats and dogs.” Both describe heavy rain.
